items.title: We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it
items.summary:
I run Tutorela , a U.S. tutoring marketplace that sells human tutoring, with AI for students between sessions. I’m saying that up front because this piece argues for that model, and because we learned the lesson behind it the hard way.

Alpha School has become the national test case for AI-first education, and it’s now expanding into public schools in Texas and South Carolina. As districts decide how much of the school day to hand to software, they should hear what happened when we gave students the best learning tool we could build.

We built it. They didn’t come. 

For 15 years we’ve run Limud Naim, a tutoring marketplace in Israel whose tutors have taught more than 500,000 private lessons. To fill the gap between those lessons, we built a math learning and practice app with more than 10,000 exercises. Every problem came with a full solution in text and video, and we made the whole thing a game, with progress and rewards, so practice would feel less like homework. A year ago we added an AI assistant that could walk a student through any step, any time, for free.

By any product standard it was the best a student could get. Only about 10% of students used it, and most of those who started didn’t stick around. The exercises were excellent and the AI was patient and clear, but none of that mattered, because the students weren’t showing up.

We’re not the only ones. 

A two-year randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools, published this year by the National Bureau of Economic Research , found the same thing with Khanmigo , Khan Academy’s AI tutor. Nearly every student…
items.t: We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it

items.title: Nvidia posts a blockbuster quarter as Jensen Huang’s dealmaking legacy hangs in the balance
items.summary:
Morgan Chittum here. Nvidia posted quarterly results late Tuesday that handily beat earnings and revenue expectations—just days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital affairs. The upheaval sent the stock to its lowest level in well over a year. The better-than-expected fiscal third quarter may give public-market investors a reprieve. But a massive question still hangs over the AI-pilled private markets, where Nvidia poured billions into investments and financing under Huang’s leadership: Will Colette Kress, the longtime CFO now serving as interim CEO, match his appetite for bankrolling the AI boom?  

Before we get to that, the numbers deserve their due: Nvidia had a very good quarter. Revenue for the three months ended October 25 came in at $115.8 billion, more than double the $57 billion recorded a year earlier and above analysts’ expectations of around $109 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, topping estimates of $2.48. The company forecasted fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—a range that clears analysts’ $125 billion estimate even at the low end. Management also raised its growth forecast for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 to 75%, from 70%.

Stratospheric revenue growth, insatiable demand for chips. It’s almost business as usual for the world’s leading AI chipmaker. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this,” Kress said. 

There’s more to the Nvidia story than blowout earnings,…
items.t: Nvidia posts a blockbuster quarter as Jensen Huang’s dealmaking legacy hangs in the balance

items.title: The seeds of the next recession are being sown in today’s booming economy, warns top economist: ‘Icarus is flying towards the sun’
items.summary:
While 2026 has been a volatile year for the U.S. economy, headline macroeconomic data tell a relatively healthy story: GDP has grown more than 2% every quarter this year—and a respectable 3.4% in Q3. The unemployment rate is steady at around 4%. And the S&P 500 is up 7% year to date.

Admittedly, inflation still looks a little hot, but with the U.S. home to the leaders of the AI revolution, it’s easy to be optimistic. What could possibly go wrong?

According to Michael Pearce, chief U.S. economist at Oxford Economics, rather a lot. In fact, Pearce believes that the currently strong expansion of the largest economy on earth means the “seeds of the next recession are being sown.”

In a note titled “Icarus is flying towards the sun,” Pearce suggests the next downturn, when it arrives, will also be “deeper and more painful” as the economy will have less of a fiscal cushion to fall back on, as government money is siphoned off by budget deficits and spiraling interest payments on the national debt.

The case for a recession stems from vulnerabilities in the economy, such as the debt levels used to finance AI spending. Goldman Sachs estimates that $500 billion in AI-related debt has been issued in 2026 thus far, and a further $420 billion will be loaned in 2027.

This presents an obvious snag if, or when, returns are slower to materialize—or don’t come to fruition at all.

The second vulnerability Pearce sees is weaker hiring among small businesses, citing Oxford Economics data tracking the share of gross job gains from existing small firms, which has fallen steadily throughout…
items.t: The seeds of the next recession are being sown in today’s booming economy, warns top economist: ‘Icarus is flying towards the sun’

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte

After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

items.title: Current price of oil as of November 18, 2026
items.summary:
At 6:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $94.21 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s a decrease of 73 cents since yesterday morning and roughly $29 more than at this time last year.

oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $94.94 -0.76% Price of oil 1 month ago $111.71 -15.66% Price of oil 1 year ago $64.96 +45.02% 

Will oil prices go up? 

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

How oil prices translate to gas pump prices 

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve 

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets…
items.t: Current price of oil as of November 18, 2026

items.title: New materials can cost 10 years and up to $100 million to discover. That ‘decade tax’ is why America’s AI boom hasn’t reached the real economy
items.summary:
IBM research notes discovering a new material can take 10 years and up to $100 million, whether it’s the alloy inside a jet engine, the coating on a chip, or the metal lining a reactor wall. That’s a decade between the first idea and the factory floor, and most ideas never make it that far.

That number should worry anyone watching the AI boom. Morgan Stanley estimates that hyperscalers and AI cloud providers will spend nearly $1.6 trillion in 2027, yet Accenture’s global CTO recently put the number of large companies truly reinvented around AI at “ basically close to zero .” Software got faster. The physical world didn’t.

I’m a materials scientist, and I spent years at an Army research lab before starting Radical AI . What’s holding AI back right now has less to do with the models than with the materials we build everything on. I call it the decade tax, and as long as we keep paying it, the AI boom will keep outrunning the economy it’s supposed to transform.

The decade tax 

The decade tax is the time and money between “we need a material that can do this” and a part that’s actually in production. Every industry that builds physical things pays it.

It exists for three reasons.

Discovery still runs on trial and error. A researcher designs a composition, makes a small batch, tests it, waits for results and adjusts. Each loop takes weeks. A good career might run a few thousand of them.

The scientific literature has grown past the point where any person can keep up with it. The AI research agents in our labs draw on 583,813 papers, more than one researcher could get…
items.t: New materials can cost 10 years and up to $100 million to discover. That ‘decade tax’ is why America’s AI boom hasn’t reached the real economy

items.title: What’s at stake for Trump and Xi in Shenzhen: A trade truce deadline, new export controls, and Iran

He then traveled to Shenzhen, where he was welcomed by Chinese President Xi Jinping for this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Forum.

Trump is scheduled to take part in three-way talks with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin while in Shenzhen. “They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace ​and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Monday, according to Reuters .

Trump’s meetings with the two leaders at APEC could test whether the U.S., China and Russia can make progress on trade and help ease tensions in the Middle East.

The talks are likely to focus on immediate economic and security concerns. Looming over the Trump-Xi meeting is a trade truce negotiated at last year’s APEC Summit, where the U.S. and China agreed to pause an escalating battle of export controls and begin a regular series of talks on trade and investment. The truce expires on Jan. 10. 

Yet Trump arrives in Shenzhen just days after Washington proposed expanding export controls on semiconductors, showing just how easily the U.S.-China relationship could tilt back into a trade war.

Given their national AI ambitions are strongly tied to investments in Nvidia and access to its coveted chips, Gulf countries will be vulnerable to any dramatic changes in its future strategy. 

During U.S. President Donald Trump’s Gulf tour in May 2025, the UAE unveiled plans to develop a 5-GW joint AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. Once complete, it will be the largest facility of its kind outside the U.S. At the heart of the project is Stargate UAE, a 1-GW computing cluster developed by Abu Dhabi-backed G42 in partnership with a host of U.S. companies, including Nvidia, which will supply its Grace Blackwell chips (GB300s). 

Nvidia has also forged a strong commercial alliance with Saudi Arabia, with Huang among a select group of U.S. tech leaders invited to meet with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his much-feted visit to the White House last November. 

During the visit, Elon Musk announced a 500-MW data center in partnership with Saudi government-backed AI company, Humain , which will be powered by Nvidia’s computing chips. 

Trump also hosted Mohammed bin Salman, alongside Huang and Elon Musk, at the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum on November 19 last year. 

Just hours later, the U.S. Commerce Department authorized the export of up to 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell GB300 chips to both G42 and Humain. Earlier in the day, Humain said it planned…

items.title: Rahm Emanuel and Chris Christie agree on one thing: character will decide 2028
items.summary:
In today’s CEO Daily: The character debate takes center stage. 

The big leadership story: Nvidia dismisses the possibility of Jensen Huang’s return. 

The markets: Stocks rebound on Nvidia’s solid earnings. 

Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . 

Good morning. Moments before I interviewed Bristol Myers Squibb CEO Chris Boerner on stage at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum yesterday, a news alert flashed across my phone: The United States had officially lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for more than 25 years. More than 5,400 cases have been reported this year alone under an administration that has fired scientists, disregarded public health protocols, and undermined faith in vaccines.

I asked Boerner, whose drug company does not make the vaccine, what he made of the news. “Very troubling,” he said, noting that America’s enviable ecosystem in biotechnology and pharmaceuticals is a benefit, not a birthright. “It rests on respect for science.”

That fireside chat took place around the same time that Jensen Huang said he’d be “honored” to return as CEO of Nvidia, as if multiple affairs and potential security violations paled next to the “outpouring of calls” for him to return. The board declined . Good call.

My conversations over the past two days reinforced that character matters, in leadership and in life. Rocket Companies founder and chairman Dan Gilbert talked about his extensive investments in transforming downtown Detroit—including The Department at Hudson’s Detroit, where the event was held. He made a compelling case for…

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

“The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report,

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

items.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?
items.summary:
Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.
